Surgical Management
Acute cholecystitis requires surgical intervention unless medi-
cally contraindicated. Without surgery, the condition may ei-
ther subside or progress to gangrene.
Medical Nutrition Therapy
Acute Cholecystitis  ​In an acute attack, oral feedings are discon-
tinued. PN may be indicated if the patient is malnourished and it 


578
PART V  Medical Nutrition Therapy
is anticipated that he or she will not be taking anything orally for 
a prolonged period. When feedings are resumed, a low-fat diet is 
recommended to decrease gallbladder stimulation. A hydrolyzed 
low-fat formula or an oral low-fat diet consisting of 30 to 45 g of 
fat per day can be given. Table 29-7 shows a fat-restricted diet.
After cholecystectomy, patients may experience symptoms 
of gastritis secondary to duodenogastric reflux of bile acids. 
The reflux also may be responsible for symptoms in this 
postcholecystectomy syndrome. At present, there are no well-
established pharmacologic approaches in the management of 
postcholecystectomy gastritis. The symptoms are not caused, 
but exacerbated, by the cholecystectomy. The addition of solu-
ble fiber to the diet may act as a sequestering agent and bind the 
bile in the stomach between meals to avoid gastritis.
